title: Where does the web map stop?
hook: Scroll a web map north and you hit an edge before the pole. Why there?

knows: that Mercator maps stretch areas near the poles
latitude from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles
doesNotKnow: that a Mercator map's height has no limit toward the poles
that square web map tiles therefore stop at about 85°

misconception: Online maps show the whole world pole to pole; the poles are just far away.
objective: The learner can explain that Mercator's height grows without limit toward the poles, so a square world map must stop where height equals width, at 85.05° north and south.
keyState: The cut has been set to 85.05° (the map exactly fills the square) and a cut beyond it (89° or the pole) has been seen with the extra map dimmed outside the square.

claims.text: Standard web map tiles (Web Mercator) draw the whole world as one square Mercator map.
claims.source: EPSG:3857 / the 'slippy map' tile scheme: zoom level 0 is one square tile covering the world in spherical Mercator (OpenStreetMap wiki, 'Slippy map tilenames'; from memory). The lesson names no product. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): EPSG:3857 slippy-map tiles: zoom 0 is a single square tile.

claims.text: A square Mercator world map stops at about 85.05° north and south.
claims.source: Height equals width when ψ(L) = π, with ψ = ln tan(45° + L/2): L = atan(sinh π) = 85.0511° (builder node run; Demo.tsx SQUARE_LAT). Matches the EPSG:3857 latitude bound (OpenStreetMap wiki; from memory) and the cm-geography brief. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: atan(sinh pi) = 85.0511 degrees.

claims.text: Mercator stretches north–south distances more and more toward the poles, so its height has no limit.
claims.source: Mercator ordinate y = R ln tan(45° + φ/2), which diverges as φ → 90° (Snyder 1987, Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, ch. 7; from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: Cut at 89°, a Mercator world map is about 1.51 times as tall as it is wide.
claims.source: ψ(89°)/π = 4.741/3.1416 = 1.509 (builder node run; Demo.tsx ratio). Quoted in the reveal only if the learner chose 89°. Other values on the stage: 75° 0.65, 80° 0.78. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: psi(89)/pi = 1.509; also 75 deg 0.645, 80 deg 0.775.

claims.text: Everything closer to the poles than 85.05° is left off a square web map.
claims.source: Follows from c1 and c2 for the zoom-0 square; tiles at every zoom subdivide the same square (OpenStreetMap wiki; from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

recall.question: Why can't a square Mercator map of the world include the North Pole?
options: The pole is ice, not land, so it is left off
Mercator's height grows without limit toward the pole, so the square must stop short
recall.why: Mercator's height grows as ln tan(45° + φ/2), which is infinite at 90°; height equals width at 85.05°, so the square stops there.
